Looking for online healthcare degrees? Compare schools and see what concentrations are available.

To spend your career in the field of health and wellness, look into online healthcare degrees. Through online study, you can learn the skills you’ll need to succeed in helping others improve their wellbeing.

You can get started by earning an online healthcare certificate, associate’s degree, or bachelor’s degree.

Here are the types of healthcare degrees you can get online. Click on one that interests you to jump to that part of the page.

Remember that you can always earn an associate’s degree and then use it to complete your bachelor’s degree later.

If mainstream medicine isn’t your thing, you might prefer to focus your studies on alternative practices and treatments. A certificate program in alternative medicine can help you demonstrate your competence in treating others using holistic or complementary approaches.

Alternative medicine includes a wide variety of practices and disciplines. Your certificate program may introduce you to massage, Chinese medicine, aromatherapy, acupuncture, yoga, qigong, or meditation. You may also learn about homeopathic medicines or natural midwifery practices.

The program may also include components on anatomy and physiology, biology and chemistry, or legal and ethical issues in alternative medicine.

Your future career path may depend on the contents of your program. You could look into being a wellness coach, a massage therapist, or a yoga instructor.

If you have additional training, an alternative medicine certificate may enhance your work as a nurse, an occupational therapist, a doctor, a mental health counselor, or a midwife.

As a dental assistant, you can contribute to helping people’s smiles gleam. Dental assistants support dentists and hygienists by taking x-rays, preparing supply trays, and getting patients ready for procedures. They may also take care of office work.

Classes in this field cover the anatomy and structure of the mouth and teeth. You may learn about dental appliances, such as dentures and dental tools.

The courses can help you learn safe practices when taking x-rays and teach you to maintain a sanitary environment so that you can reduce the spread of infections among staff or patients. You may also learn to use dental software and imaging tools.

After completing your program, which may take up to a year, you can take a certification exam. Once you meet your state’s requirements, you can practice as a Certified Dental Assistant (CDA).

Dental assistants make an average of $41,180 per year (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

Are you curious about sports medicine and physical therapy and wondering if this is the right line of work for you? Instead of jumping right into a program to become a physical therapist, consider enrolling in a certificate program.

The courses can provide the training you need to work as an aide in a physical therapy or sports medicine office.

Your program should familiarize you with the basics of what happens in a medical office. For example, you may study privacy laws, billing practices, and record maintenance. You’ll also need to learn about human anatomy, physiology, and kinesiology.

As a physical therapy aide, you may earn about $28,450 each year (Bureau of Labor Statistics). You could stick with this line of work or choose to advance your career with more education.

Getting an associate’s degree is the next step to moving into an assistant role. To become a full-fledged physical therapist, you’ll need a doctoral degree.

To get started as a patient caregiver and keeper of records, consider earning a two-year degree in medical assisting. This associate’s degree can qualify you to carry out essential tasks that support the work of the doctors and nurses in your medical practice.

You’ll need to study human anatomy, health procedures, and medications. Your coursework will probably include requirements for hands-on experiences so that you can practice your clinical skills.

In addition to helping with patient care and procedures, medical assistants often do office work, so you’ll need to study insurance, billing, and coding. You may get to try out some common database systems for recording patient data and organizing records.

Medical assistants can work in doctor’s offices, healthcare clinics, hospitals, and surgical centers. The average salary for this job is $35,850 per year, and the number of positions is projected to rise at a rate of about 19% over the next 10 years (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

Medical coders are responsible for maintaining accurate patient records and billing documents. If you are detail-oriented, good with computers, and interested in working in a medical setting, then a degree in medical coding could be for you.

Coursework in this field typically start with foundational classes that introduce terms used in healthcare settings and basic information about procedures, treatments, and medications.

You should also study classifications and codes for medical procedures and explore the systems that are used for recording them. Lessons on patient privacy and healthcare ethics are likely to be important parts of your program as well.

After completing your program, you’ll need to take the Certified Coding Associate exam. Medical coders often work in the office of healthcare offices or hospitals, but some may work from home.

The average salary for medical records and health information technicians is $44,090 per year. Jobs in this field have a projected growth rate of about 8% for the next decade (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

When a medical office is staffed by competent, efficient professionals, it can help operations throughout the facility run more smoothly. To take on this important responsibility, you can earn a two-year online degree in medical office administration.

You’ll need to take classes like Medical Office Terminology, Insurance and Reimbursement, and Billing Practices. The courses may include practice sessions with medical database software.

Additionally, you may have classes on other software programs, such as applications for word processing or bookkeeping. Learning to use legal and ethical business practices should be a key part of your curriculum, and you may have a whole class focused on patient privacy.

Your studies may qualify you to take the Certified Medical Administrative Assistant exam. With your training, you could become a medical secretary, making an average annual salary of around $37,350 (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

Other potential job titles include billing secretary, intake clerk, medical receptionist, or administrative assistant.

If you’d like to provide a friendly face and helpful services for patients who are picking up prescriptions, then consider a career as a pharmacy tech.

When you study for a pharmacy technician associate’s degree, you can acquire skills for assisting pharmacists and taking care of many of the jobs that go on behind a pharmacy counter.

Your first classes for this major should provide introductions to medical terminology, pharmacy practices, and tech responsibilities.

After that, you need to study drug categories, pharmacy structures, ethical issues, and safe and hygienic practices. You’ll need to use math skills to calculate medication dosages. The program may include clinical experiences so you can try out your skills in a real pharmacy.

After completing your associate’s degree, you may be eligible to take the Pharmacy Technician Certification Board exam. Working as a pharmacy tech, you might earn a salary of about $35,100 per year (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

Thanks to technology, healthcare facilities, companies, and even individuals have more medical data at their fingertips than ever before.

Making good use of that data requires trained professionals who know how to store, organize, and retrieve information. With a degree in health informatics, you can become that expert.

The curriculum for this program involves both business and healthcare classes. On the business side, you may study information technology, spreadsheets, accounting, and management.

To prepare you for jobs in the healthcare system, you’ll likely take classes on anatomy, medical terminology, medical coding, pharmacology, health insurance, privacy laws, and public health.

After graduation, you could become an informatics specialist in a healthcare organization. You might be able to work as a medical or health services manager, which commands an average annual salary of $104,280 (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

Instead of working for a medical organization, you might be hired by an insurance, healthcare technology, or pharmaceutical company.

For a flexible healthcare bachelor’s degree, consider studying health sciences. This program can set you up for success in clinical or administrative healthcare roles, or it can lay a good foundation for further professional training.

As the program name implies, you can expect this to be a science-heavy program; you may need to take chemistry, microbiology, physics, and anatomy. You’ll also need to study medical terminology, health insurance reimbursement, nutrition, and psychology.

Health sciences majors have many career options. You might become a health services manager or a medical administrator. Other ideas include health education, medical supply sales, or insurance work.

To work directly with patients, you could become a registrar at a treatment facility or take a technician or assistant role.

Alternatively, many students choose to continue their education after earning this degree; you might enter a professional program for becoming a physician assistant, an audiologist, a pharmacist, or a dentist.

Health services majors are capable of handling many of the behind-the-scenes, administrative, or research tasks in medical or community organizations.

You could choose this major if your goal is to get a versatile overview of the healthcare system. It can also be a good choice if you already have professional medical training — for example, a medical assistant associate’s degree — and want to take your education to the next level.

The classes for this program may cover topics like global health and healthcare delivery systems. The curriculum can help you develop your management and project-development skills.

You may be able to choose a specialty area to enhance your expertise in a particular aspect of the healthcare field; options may include gerontology, administration, or community health.

With this degree, you could be a health educator or run community health programs. You could also work as an administrator in a medical or long-term care facility.

Healthcare administrators keep medical facilities running smoothly. Their work ensures that there is coordination among staff members, office tasks are efficiently accomplished, quality is maintained throughout the practice, and the organization is moving in a positive direction.

You can prepare for such a position by earning a bachelor’s degree in healthcare administration online.

For this degree, you may take multiple courses about the business of healthcare; the topics may include finance, economics, insurance, human relations, communication, and marketing.

Other classes may address epidemiology, public health, data collection, and health policies. You may have the option to select a concentration like leadership, information management, or quality assurance.

After graduation, you could become a medical services administrator in a hospital, a clinic, a residential facility, or a government agency. Seeking a higher administrative role could be more rewarding and could make pursuing a master’s degree in healthcare administration worth it.

You could also perform administrative duties for a pharmaceutical company. Another path to consider is working as a community health manager who oversees outreach programs.

If you’re interested in helping people keep their minds healthy, then you should think about studying mental health counseling. This degree program can serve as a stepping stone toward becoming a licensed mental health counselor.

This degree involves the study of various branches of psychology, such as social, cognitive, and abnormal psychology. It also introduces counseling techniques and assessment procedures and may discuss working among diverse or multicultural populations.

Once you have this degree, you may be able to work as a mental health technician who performs supportive services under the supervision of a licensed counselor. Other ideas are working as a caregiver in a residential facility or coordinating cases for social-services clients.

If you want to become a licensed counselor, you’ll need to continue on for a master’s degree in clinical mental health counseling or a related field.

Do you dream of becoming a nurse? Getting your Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN) can prepare you to enter this field and set you up for future advancement.

The curriculum should cover the basics of nursing practice and clinical care. Common topics of study include wellness, diseases, injuries, medications, and treatment procedures.

Other courses may cover health informatics, ethical practices, and leadership in nursing. You’ll probably need to gain hands-on experience by doing practicum work in a healthcare facility near you.

After graduation, you’ll need to take the National Council Licensure Examination. As a licensed nurse, you might earn around $75,330 annually (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

If you’re already an RN, don’t rule out the idea of getting your BSN. Earning your bachelor’s degree can help you move up in your field and secure positions of greater responsibility. You can fast-track your degree by seeking out an online program designed specifically for RN-to-BSN study.

If eating well-balanced meals and helping others achieve optimal health through food is important to you, then you might make a great nutritionist or dietitian. Get ready for these careers by earning an online bachelor’s degree in nutritional sciences.

You may take classes like Chemistry, which relates to the composition of food, and Behavioral Science, which can help you understand the basis for people’s food choices.

You can study how to evaluate the health benefits of various foods and discuss ways that dietary needs change throughout the lifetime. Other courses can teach you to provide nutritional counseling for clients. Some schools require an internship experience.

A butcher is a tradesperson who specializes in meatcutting, breaking down animal carcasses into primal cuts, preparation and retailing of meat, and sometimes slaughtering animals, or participates within any combination of these tasks.[1] They may prepare standard cuts of meat and poultry for sale in retail or wholesale food establishments. A butcher may be employed by supermarkets, grocery stores, butcher shops and fish markets, slaughterhouses, or may be self-employed.[2]

Butchery is an ancient trade, whose duties may date back to the domestication of livestock; butchering guilds were first formed in England as far back as 1272.[3] In England during the Middle Ages, butchering was heavily regulated and structured. Butchers operated in a broad network of urban trade systems, some of these were food provision, textiles, clothing, etc. These trades overlapped and allowed for interconnected systems to form in medieval towns.[4] The different trade regulations maintained the quality of meat and ostensibly protected the public. The butchering was regulated by appointed officials, specifically when it came to the sale and preparation of the meat.[5] These regulations were used to make sure they met the standards to be sold to the public.[5] These regulations represent earlier efforts to maintain quality standards in public spaces and markets.

Despite earlier attempts and regulations, butchers were still associated with air contamination and ‘putrid’ meat.[6] Historical accounts commonly show a similar complaint of butchers disposing of the waste of their butchering into public spaces. These complaints linked the disposal of the waste to diseases and bad smells. Authorities took these disposals as serious offences and were punished accordingly. These punishments were to deter such practices,[6] and contributed to restricting instances of improper disposal. When they would occur, they were sometimes associated to widespread animal diseases when it became difficult to ensure the quality of meat.[6]

Through medieval England to the Renaissance, the butchering trade became closely tied to guilds systems in urban communities. Guilds played a big role in regulations and market organization and economic activity. They often played bigger roles in bigger urban settings such as cities or large towns.[7] During this period, efforts were made to regulate and standardize the butchering trade.[7]Authorities also became more involved in the regulation of guilds and butchering to ensure they continued to perform with quality in mind. The authorities would be very involved in making sure that underweighting of the meat would not occur, so the price of the meat would be fair to the public.[7] This caused tension between the butchers and regulators, especially in times of changing market conditions.[7]

By the nineteenth century, industrialisation brought major changes to the meat industry and the butchering profession. Slaughterhouses increasingly located to designated industrial facilities away from public spaces. Prior to this shift butchering was typical to see in public.[8] This caused a bigger rift between butchering and the public, as it was starting to no longer be popular to go to butcher shops nor see the process of the butchering.[8] Industrial facilities were often seen as more sanitary,[8] as they were seen to have more regulations. This led to the foundation of what we now know today of the relationships between the meat industry, butchers, and the public.

Since the 20th century, many countries and local jurisdictions offer trade certifications for butchers to ensure quality, safety, and health standards but not all butchers have formal certification or training. Trade qualification in English-speaking countries is often earned through an apprenticeship although some training organisations also certify their students. In Canada, once a butcher is trade qualified, they can learn to become a master butcher (Fleishmaster).[9][10]

Standards and practices of butchery differ between countries, regions and ethnic groups. Variation with respect to the types of animals that are butchered as well as the cuts and parts of the animal that are sold depends on the types of foods that are prepared by the butcher's customers.

Butchery is a traditional line of work. In the industrialized world, slaughterhouses use butchers to slaughter the animals, performing one or a few of the steps repeatedly as specialists on a semi-automated disassembly line. The steps include stunning (rendering the animal incapacitated), exsanguination (severing the carotid or brachial arteries to facilitate blood removal), skinning (removing the hide or pelt) or scalding and dehairing (pork), evisceration (removing the viscera) and splitting (dividing the carcass in half longitudinally).

After the carcasses are chilled (unless "hot-boned"), primary butchery consists of selecting carcasses, sides, or quarters from which primal cuts can be produced with the minimum of wastage; separating the primal cuts from the carcass; trimming primal cuts and preparing them for secondary butchery or sale; and storing cut meats. Secondary butchery involves boning, trimming and value-adding of primal cuts in preparation for sale. Historically, primary and secondary butchery were performed in the same establishment, but the advent of methods of preservation (vacuum packing) and low cost transportation has largely separated them.

In parts of the world, it is common for butchers to perform many or all of the butcher's duties. Where refrigeration is less common, these skills are required to sell the meat of slaughtered animals.

Butchers sell their goods in specialized stores, commonly termed a butcher shop (American English), butchery (South African English) or butchers (British English). Butchers at a butcher shop may perform primary butchery, but will typically perform secondary butchery to prepare fresh cuts of meat for sale. These shops may also sell related products, such as Charcuterie, hot food (using their own meat products), food preparation supplies, baked goods and grocery items. Butcher shops can have a wider variety of animal types, meat cuts and quality of cuts. Additionally, butcher shops may focus on a particular culture, or nationality, of meat production. Some butcher shops, termed "meat delis", may also include a delicatessen.

In the United States and Canada, butcher shops have become less common because of the increasing popularity of supermarkets and warehouse clubs. Many remaining ones are aimed at Hispanic and other immigrants or, more recently, those looking for organic offerings.[11] Supermarkets employ butchers for secondary butchery, but in the United States even that role is diminished with the advent of "case-ready" meat, where the product is packaged for retail sale at the packinghouse or specialized central processing plants. [citation needed]

Hot boning is a process used by butchers to remove the meat from the carcass almost instantly after the animal is slaughtered. This is done to prevent rigor mortis (Chemical changes causing stiffening of the limbs and corpse). Warm meat is often softer and easier to remove from the bone, and hot boning can save refrigeration costs. Cattle, Lamb, and Pigs are the animals most frequently hot boned.[12]

Popularity and relevance of the art of butchering have shifted over the years both geographically and historically. Meat demand has risen dramatically over the centuries, but in many Western countries, like the United States, Butcher shops are less prevalent. Meat markets have grown by an average 5.1% per year since 1970, and this is largely due to urbanization and demand. In the United States, meat is mass-produced and then shipped to stores that can sell large amounts quickly and keep the meat frozen. Individual butcher shops with contracts to small farms struggle to keep their prices low enough to match large industries.[13]

Butcher shops are still common in many European and South American countries. In countries like Argentina meat consumption was as high as 97 kilograms per person in 2002, with the vast majority of it being beef.[14]

In asian countries, butchering consists of more "nose to tail" butchering practices, which involves using every part of the animal, including common parts that are typically thrown away in the West, like pig blood, chicken feet, rabbit head, tripe, and tendon. Often these meats are harvested with specialty knives like the Caidao, hankatsu, and honesuki.

In the United States and in other western countries, many customers have become familiar with meat departments in grocery stores and supermarkets rather than butcher shops. Meat departments are used to sell and take in more product faster and more efficiently. Butchers who work in meat departments have tasks like small scale cutting and cleaning, as well as marinating, packaging and ordering shipments of meat. Butchers in meat departments almost never assist in the slaughtering process.[15]

Most meat departments sell fresh (never frozen) cuts of meat. Many butchers are able to manipulate the "bloom" aspect of meat (the bright red color of steaks that looks fresh). When meat is first cut, it will appear purple. This is due to a surplus of myoglobin on the surface; once the meat has first warmed up to room temperature, oxygen is added to the meat to oxidize myoglobin, which produces oxymyoglobin, giving the meat the scarlet red color that consumers indicate as fresh. Through this process, supermarkets and meat departments are able to make meat appear fresh for longer periods of time. This process is referred to as "blooming".[16]

A primal cut is a piece of meat initially separated from the carcass during butchering. Different countries and cultures make these cuts in different ways, and primal cuts also differ between type of carcass. The British, American and French primal cuts all differ in some respects. One notable example with pork is fatback, which in Europe is an important primal cut of pork, but in North America is regarded as trimmings to be used in sausage or rendered into lard. The primal cuts may be sold complete or cut further.

In various periods and cultures, the term "butcher" has been applied to people who act cruelly to other human beings or slaughter them. For example, Pompey, a prominent Roman general and politician of the first century BC, got the Latin nickname adulescentulus carnifex, translated as "The Teenage Butcher" or "The Butcher Boy", due to brutal treatment of political opponents in the early part of his career. More recently, the Bosslot Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić was nicknamed "the Butcher of the Balkans".

The term can also be used in a semi-humorous or metaphorical way to describe someone whose actions resemble the various skills and methods of a butcher (chopping, cutting, slicing, stabbing etc.) Spanish footballer Andoni Goikoetxea was popularly ascribed the epithet "The Butcher of Bilbao" in recognition of his perceived aggressive style of play and frequent, sometimes injurious, challenges on opposing players.

With election denialists installed in key positions, officials using series of measures to change voting rules

The Trump administration is waging war on voting rights using justice department lawsuits, FBI investigations and an executive order to limit voting by mail, moves mirroring the US president’s false claims he lost the 2020 election due to voting fraud, say election experts and ex-officials.

Since Donald Trump began his second term, numerous 2020 election denialists have been installed in key agencies such as the Department of Justice, the FBI and elsewhere to pursue widely discredited claims of fraud, which can intimidate election workers and voters in swing states that Trump lost to Joe Biden in 2020.

The justice department has also filed lawsuits seeking sensitive voter data from 30 states – even though, by law, states control elections – and the FBI has launched investigations into debunked allegations of voting fraud in Georgia, Wisconsin and a few other swing states that Trump lost in 2020.

Trump in late March this year issued an executive order sharply tightening mail-in voting rules, which Trump has long claimed without evidence contribute to fraud. The order gives the United States Postal Service unprecedented powers to issue new rules making voting by mail harder.

The administration’s multi-pronged push to change voting rules is under way despite laws that empower states and Congress to set election rules, sparking lawsuits from states and non-partisan voting rights groups.

In early April, for instance, officials from 23 Democratic states including California and Washington DC filed a lawsuit to block Trump’s executive order to curb voting by mail, arguing that the order was an unconstitutional effort to interfere with states administering their elections.

The administration’s aggressive steps to tighten voting rules come as Trump and many Republican allies have voiced strong fears that the November midterm elections are likely to give Democrats control of the House, and possibly the Senate too, limiting Trump’s powers and possibly leading to his impeachment again.

At a Republican House retreat in January, Trump stressed the stakes were high for his future if Democrats win control of the House. “You gotta win the midterms, because if we don’t win the midterms, it’s just gonna be … I mean, they’ll find a reason to impeach me,” Trump told lawmakers.

Former federal officials with voting expertise are sharply critical of the Trump administration’s moves to limit voting rights with phoney charges of voting fraud.

“The Department of Justice has no authority to sweep up the voter rolls, which contain private information like driver’s licenses and social security numbers, from every state in the nation,” Eileen O’Connor, a senior counsel with the Brennan Center who spent eight years in the justice department’s voting section of the civil rights division, told the Guardian.

“The department has 30 active lawsuits against states and the District of Columbia to force the turnover of these sensitive records. So far, eight courts have issued rulings in these cases, and the DoJ has lost each one.”

O’Connor stressed that “lawsuits against the states are only one part of a broader campaign by the Trump administration to interfere with elections. The administration has targeted election officials, attempted to rewrite election rules, pardoned January 6 rioters, and elevated election deniers.

“It has also raised the prospect of deploying federal immigration agents at polling sites – but federal law explicitly bans federal officers from interfering in elections and prohibits armed federal agents from being deployed anywhere an election is held.”

Other ex-election officials voice alarms about Trump’s moves to revamp voting rules and curb voting rights.

“Trump continues to falsely claim that voting by foreign nationals, which is illegal and rarely occurs, and practices such as mail-in voting resulted in a fraudulent election in 2020 and will result in the 2026 midterm elections being rigged against Republicans,” Larry Noble, a former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission who now teaches law at the American University, told the Guardian. “However, numerous audits and lawsuits have failed to find any meaningful fraud in the 2020 election.”

Noble added: “Trump apparently believes that Democrats winning an election is proof enough that there was fraud because, as Trump has brazenly charged, “[I]f they didn’t cheat, they could not win …”

Such criticism has not deterred Trump and top officials at the justice department and other key agencies from claiming the voting changes and investigations they are pursuing are needed to combat what they falsely insist was widespread voting fraud in 2020. The acting attorney general Todd Blanche, for instance, told Fox News last month there was “a ton of evidence that the election was rigged” in 2020.

In a potential harbinger of voting fraud charges ahead in the fall elections if Trump doesn’t like the results, Trump quickly claimed that California’s early June primaries were rigged when Spencer Pratt, a Trump-backed mayoral candidate in Los Angeles, lost an early voting lead in the nation’s largest state, where final results often take longer to tabulate.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that it was “Not possible for Spencer Pratt to have lost the L.A. runoffs after the big lead he had… 3rd World Nation.”

Further, soon after the primaries were held Trump claimed without details that they were “under investigation by the US attorney’s office in Los Angeles”. The justice department also sent a federal prosecutor to observe ballot processing in Los Angeles.

The justice department’s heavy tilt to election denialism became palpable soon after Trump took office in 2025 as the department’s voting section in the civil rights division was revamped to align with Trump’s election denialist views and its staff was sharply reduced last year from about 30 lawyers to less than half that number, according to a former Department of Justice lawyer.

To implement Trump-backed changes in voting rules and curb voting rights, the justice department has recruited a number of new lawyers whose résumés include efforts to fight Trump’s 2020 loss to Joe Biden.

The justice department in April, for instance, tapped the ex-Republican congressman Dan Bishop of North Carolina, an avid election denier in 2020 who had been serving as a US attorney in his state for just five months, to lead a national drive to ferret out voting fraud including debunked allegations from 2020.

In related moves, Democracy Docket disclosed in May that William Mohrman, a Minneapolis lawyer who was involved in lawsuits that sought to overturn Biden’s victory, had been hired as a senior counsel by the justice department’s voting section, according to court filings.

Court documents show that Mohrman entered his first appearance on behalf of the government in a lawsuit seeking Georgia’s unredacted statewide voter registration records from 2020.

Mohrman is one of a growing list of attorneys the section added since 2025 who were involved in 2020 election challenges or who worked with well-known election deniers. Among others, the current acting head of the section, former California prosecutor Eric Neff, reportedly has various links to election-conspiracy promoters.

These new hires coincide with shifts in the justice department’s voting section away from its traditional priority of voting rights enforcement towards lawsuits seeking sensitive voter records from states and counties nationwide. In another big break from non-partisan traditions, the Department of Justice last year backed the legality of a Texas redistricting plan that could help Republicans pick up five House seats in the midterms, while it challenged unsuccessfully a California redistricting plan voters approved that could help Democrats win five seats.

On another election front that tracks Trump’s bogus voting-fraud claims, the FBI has made investigating 2020 voting fraud a growing priority. The FBI has active inquiries into voting fraud in 2020 in Georgia and Wisconsin which critics say perpetuate lies about Trump’s loss and may intimidate election workers and voters.

This year, the FBI raided an election hub in Fulton county, Georgia, seized election data and images of ballots in Arizona, demanded ballots in Michigan, and in May expanded its inquiries to include the Milwaukee, Wisconsin area, according to the Washington Post.

FBI agents, the Post reported, visited homes of former and current Wisconsin election officials as part of an investigation into discredited election conspiracy theories pushed by Trump.

The FBI has tried for months to seize ballots, obtain access to poll workers’ personal information, and talk to election officials in swing states, moves that mirror Trump’s debunked claims that he won the 2020 election.

Elsewhere, Trump’s March 2026 executive order on voting by mail has ignited a firestorm of lawsuits and alarms from voting experts.

The gist of the order charges the USPS with deciding who may vote by mail and authorizes it not to deliver ballots sent by individuals who are not included on newly developed federal mail voter lists. The order, ominously, threatens criminal penalties for election workers, mail carriers and others who deliver or send ballots to people the administration claims are ineligible.

In a related step, the order instructs the Department of Homeland Security to develop lists of citizens in every state using unreliable and incomplete federal data materials. The Brennan Center and other voting rights advocates have warned that if implemented, the order would create chaos and curb voting by eligible US citizens.

The Brennan Center and other groups, both non-partisan and partisan, as well as states, have challenged the executive order in court, just as they challenged Trump’s March 2025 executive order changing key voting rules.

To date, several federal courts have blocked major parts of Trump’s 2025 order that would require citizens to show a passport or similar document to register to vote, which the administration has appealed.

Notably, some Republican veterans also foresee big risks with Trump’s executive orders on voting.

“These attempts are clearly unconstitutional. States run elections, not the feds. One executive order even directs the US Postal Service to decide which voters can receive mail-in ballots and which not, as if they could manage such an assignment,” said the veteran Republican consultant Charlie Black.

Noble warned: “Trump’s executive order requiring the Department of Homeland Security to compile a list of verified US citizens eligible to vote and the Postal Service to limit mail-in voting, could very well disenfranchise millions of voters while doing nothing to eliminate virtually non-existent voter fraud.”

In Noble’s eyes, “Trump is using lies to justify an unprecedented effort to have the federal government take over the administration of elections, despite the constitution giving the states that power.”

A class is a specialized role chosen for the player character upon starting the game. Each one has a different starting set of stats, equipment, and abilities. These alternative ways of starting can drastically change the beginning of the game and the player experience. However, the starting class does not determine the final role of a character. All starting classes may raise stats and progress through the game in a way that allows them to use all equipment and abilities once requirements are met.

Click on any of the class names to receive a more detailed overview of the respective class.

Disregarding the Resistance figure, all classes start with a total of 71 stat points plus one per Soul Level; this is worth noting because Resistance is usually considered useless and not beneficial to level. A class should not be chosen solely based upon who has the most points at SL1 - any class that doesn't have useless stats for a chosen build is just as good as any other.

In Dark Souls, the character plays the role of an undead. Most undead are hollow (lost their humanity and will attack anything), and all are labeled pariahs by the society of the Dark Souls world. Hollowing can be reversed by offering humanity at bonfires, making the player character appear human. Being human allows players to access certain multiplayer features, such as summoning phantoms (co-op), invading other players, or being invaded by phantoms (PVP).

Choosing a class does not determine the character's later role or style, it merely gives the player character a set of starting stats and equipment, note however that every class has its strengths and weaknesses that require some time to get used to.

Melee combat is required, but magic and ranged combat are options as well, especially if the engagement of higher-powered foes early on is desired. Magic is mostly learned from trainers. Early Miracles are taught by Petrus of Thorolund, Sorceries by Griggs of Vinheim and Pyromancies by Laurentius of the Great Swamp. Petrus is first met at the Firelink Shrine, the game's hub, while Griggs is rescued from Lower Undead Burg and Laurentius from the depths. Later more advanced trainers will appear. A catalyst and the Soul Arrow sorcery can be purchased immediately after arriving in Firelink from blacksmith Rickert in the New Londo Ruins.

Note that using magic makes combat significantly easier in the overworld since you can snipe enemies from afar and 'bait' or 'kite' single enemies away from a group. Bosses, on the other hand, may prove more difficult if sniping isn't an option. Some bosses like to get very personal, and your physical defense if starting as a sorcerer or cleric will be significantly weaker than melee combat starting options.

Bows are rarely useful in combat but are suitable for stationary foes and to pull enemies. A Short Bow can be purchased early from the Undead Merchant in Undead Burg. Purchasing this bow and about 60-70 arrows allows the Drake Sword, an incredibly powerful sword, to be obtained early - however, note that this sword lacks scaling, meaning that it quickly becomes useless due to its flat damage (this means that the sword's damage is stationary regardless of character level or stats). Crossbows are less useful than bows in such cases because they cannot be manually aimed.

Another way to utilize the bow is poison. Most larger enemies have a limited range of aggression. With this in mind, most enemies can be poisoned/sniped from afar without difficulty.

Unlike Demon's Souls, items are used to write (and rate) comments, create a summoning sign or invade. The Orange Guidance Soapstone (to write and rate messages) is purchased from the Undead Merchant in Undead Burg, the White Sign Soapstone (to offer help in co-op) is given by Solaire of Astora if the player agrees to assist him, and Cracked Red Eye Orbs (for invading) are available throughout the world.

Dark Souls is non-linear, and there are many effective ways to play and options for where to go. Experimenting with different weapons, spells, and techniques will help you decide what you like. There is no single best weapon or Covenant.

Note that despite Dark Souls' being famous for "being extremely difficult," if you're experiencing insurmountable difficulties, perhaps trying another set of equipment, weapons, spells or routes is worth a try.

Keep in mind that the game will reward players who explore and experiment and are willing to change their tactics to overcome difficulties, but will punish those who remain stubborn and make mistakes.
Try to think outside of the box if you're facing obstacles!

The food and beverage manufacturing sector operates under a compliance burden that no other industry matches — FSMA preventive controls, HACCP critical control point monitoring, allergen sanitation verification, FDA 21 CFR Part 117 documentation, and multi-scheme food safety certifications including SQF, BRC Global Standards, FSSC 22000, and IFS Food. A general-purpose CMMS deployed in a food processing plant without food-safety-specific configuration creates dangerous documentation gaps: maintenance records that don't map to HACCP plans, sanitation schedules that aren't linked to allergen changeover protocols, and PM completion data that can't be exported in the format FDA or third-party auditors require.

The best CMMS for food manufacturing in 2026 must do more than schedule preventive maintenance work orders. It must integrate with HACCP prerequisite programs, enforce sanitation standard operating procedures (SSOPs) at the work order level, track food-contact surface maintenance separately from non-food-contact equipment, and maintain an immutable compliance audit trail that survives personnel turnover and system migrations. Before comparing platforms, food plant maintenance managers must align on the non-negotiable feature requirements that separate a food-grade CMMS from a generic industrial maintenance platform. The evaluation criteria below reflect the operational and regulatory reality of food and beverage manufacturing in 2026.

FSMA compliance requires that equipment maintenance activities tied to food safety preventive controls — temperature control systems, CCP monitoring equipment, allergen contact surface assets — be documented with corrective action records linked to the preventive control plan. A food manufacturing CMMS must allow maintenance records to be tagged to specific FSMA preventive controls with automatic escalation when PM tasks are overdue on food safety-critical assets.

HACCP-integrated maintenance workflows ensure that calibration records for CCP monitoring instruments — temperature probes, pH meters, metal detectors, checkweighers — are automatically linked to the HACCP plan, with out-of-calibration alerts that trigger corrective action work orders before the affected CCP monitoring equipment is returned to service. HACCP CMMS software closes the loop between maintenance activity and food safety control.

Sanitation scheduling in food and beverage plants must manage allergen changeover cleaning, daily sanitation of food-contact surfaces, pre-operational equipment inspections, and periodic deep-cleaning cycles — all with digital sign-off records that satisfy FDA documentation requirements. The best food factory CMMS platforms support SSOP-linked sanitation work orders that capture chemical concentration, contact time, rinse verification, and employee sign-off in a single auditable record.

Food safety auditors conducting SQF, BRC, FSSC 22000, or regulatory inspections require instant access to maintenance history, calibration records, sanitation logs, and corrective action records organized by asset, date range, and compliance category. A food industry maintenance software platform must generate audit-ready compliance reports without requiring manual data compilation — reducing audit preparation time from days to hours.

Regulatory and food safety certification requirements differentiate maintenance procedures, lubricant specifications, and inspection frequencies for food-contact and non-food-contact equipment. A food plant CMMS must support asset classification that automatically applies food-grade maintenance standards — including NSF H1 food-grade lubricant requirements and food-contact surface sanitation verification — to correctly classified assets throughout the PM program.

Food and beverage plant maintenance technicians performing PM tasks, sanitation checks, and equipment inspections in GMP-controlled areas require mobile-first CMMS interfaces that work reliably in environments with limited connectivity. Mobile work order execution with barcode/QR scanning for asset identification, photo capture for maintenance documentation, and offline mode with automatic sync when connectivity resumes is a baseline requirement for modern F&B CMMS deployment.

The food and beverage CMMS market has consolidated around a set of platforms that offer meaningful food-safety-specific functionality beyond generic maintenance scheduling. The comparison below evaluates the leading options against the criteria that matter most to food plant engineers and maintenance managers responsible for FSMA compliance, HACCP documentation, and multi-scheme food safety certification maintenance.

The FDA Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA) Preventive Controls for Human Food rule under 21 CFR Part 117 establishes specific documentation requirements for maintenance activities that are part of a food facility's food safety preventive control plan. Understanding what FSMA actually requires from a maintenance documentation perspective is essential for evaluating whether a candidate CMMS platform will satisfy regulatory scrutiny during FDA inspections. Book a demo to see how OxMaint maps your maintenance program directly to FSMA preventive control documentation requirements.

FSMA requires written records of preventive control monitoring, corrective actions, and verification activities for food safety preventive controls that include equipment maintenance as a control measure. Maintenance records for equipment involved in process controls — temperature-controlled cooking, pasteurization, metal detection — must demonstrate that the equipment was maintained in a condition that supports the food safety function it performs. A FSMA compliant CMMS automatically links PM completion records to the specific preventive controls they support.

When maintenance activities reveal equipment conditions that could compromise food safety — a failed temperature probe on a pasteurizer, a damaged food-contact surface on a filling line, a metal detector that fails calibration — FSMA requires documented corrective action records that identify the problem, describe the corrective action taken, evaluate affected product for safety, and prevent recurrence. A food safety CMMS must generate corrective action work orders that capture all required data elements in a format that satisfies FDA records review.

Food facilities that use contract maintenance service providers for specialized equipment maintenance must maintain records of contractor activity that are as complete and accessible as records from in-house maintenance staff. A food beverage CMMS software platform must support contractor work order management with the same documentation standards applied to internal maintenance — including sign-off, time stamps, parts used, and compliance verification — creating a unified maintenance record regardless of who performed the work.

Sanitation scheduling in food and beverage manufacturing is not a simple recurring task — it is a risk-managed program that must account for allergen changeover protocols, cleaning-in-place (CIP) validation, environmental monitoring integration, pre-operational inspection requirements, and the zoning complexity of facilities producing multiple product lines with different allergen and microbial risk profiles. The best food processing maintenance platforms treat sanitation as a first-class maintenance discipline — not an afterthought bolted onto a generic work order system. Try OxMaint free to see how sanitation scheduling integrates with your full F&B maintenance program in one platform.

Allergen changeover cleaning requires verification steps — visual inspection, ATP swabbing, allergen-specific swab testing — that must be documented and signed off before the production line can be released for the next allergen profile. A food-grade CMMS must enforce allergen changeover sanitation workflows with mandatory verification capture and block work order completion until all required verification steps are recorded, preventing inadvertent allergen cross-contact through incomplete sanitation.

Cleaning-in-place systems in food and beverage facilities require regular maintenance of spray devices, chemical dosing systems, heat exchangers, and flow controls — with validation records that demonstrate CIP cycles deliver the required time, temperature, chemical concentration, and flow velocity parameters at food-contact surfaces. For a seriously stylish home away from home, without giving up hotel comforts, look no further than The Guesthouse Hotel. The elegant, characterful suites are fully self-sufficient—you get a chic, colorful living room, a fully functional kitchen, a comfortable bedroom, and even your private balcony with a view of the city—along with perks of a 24/7 reception and impeccable, warm service.

The atmosphere is neighborly with all the homely comforts, but the hotel still has just enough pizzazz to make it feel like a special place to stay. And when contrasted to the ultra-modern skyrises you find in downtown, The Guesthouse stands out as a one-of-a-kind, intentionally residential spot. Here’s what we thought of it.

Stepping inside The Guesthouse Hotel and you’ll forget all the usual noise usually plaguing city hotel lobbies. From the reception desk to the library and club room, the Guesthouse’s common spaces are quiet, sophisticated, but avoid feeling stuffy: you’ll find printed artwork on the walls, sleekly designed sofas, and shelves full of local artisans’ products. The library’s old leather-bound tomes sit next to board games that guests are encouraged to pick up, take up their rooms, or play wherever they wish—it’s a very cosy vibe.

The original building (today home to the 3-bedroom suites) was purchased by a couple to be turned into luxury condos, and set to go on the market in 2008. As the financial crash took its toll on the housing market, the condos took on a new lease of life as guest accommodation. Quirky touches bring personality to what could otherwise have been a concrete slab—all the wood furnishing in the lobby, library, and club room comes from a raised barn farm in Wisconsin, adding a touch of countryside, which is a nod the upbringing of the owners in rural Illinois.

The Hotel has 25 suites, divided in single, double, and triple bed, and each is equipped with an open kitchen with a granite breakfast counter (and an ice machine in the spacious fridge), a washer and dryer, and stylish bathroom. I stayed in the two bedroom, two bathroom suite, which sleeps up to four, making it ideal for families and friends, with one king bed in the main room, and one queen bed in the secondary. Unlike one-bed suites, the two-bed has a bathtub. You can pick a front-door facing room for peaceful views over the St Boniface Catholic cemetery or, like me, opt for the smaller second room for top cosyness and a glimpse of the city skyline. Both rooms have ample built-in wardrobes, ideal for those planning a longer stay.

The high-ceiling living room is adorned with velveteen sofas and flooded by natural light thanks to the big windows and adjacent private balcony—which is a dreamy spot to enjoy your morning coffee, if you ask me.

While the hotel doesn’t have food and drink facilities, it’s nestled on the doorstep of Chicago’s North Side, which has plenty to whet your appetite. The surrounding blocks are home to a plethora of small cafes and intimate diners, and if you want to swap your kitchen counter basket for something a little heartier, visit traditional American-style Dollop Diner.

For something a little flashier, head to Andersonville for bistros and more upmarket restaurants, including Taiwanese Minyoli and Bar Roma, great for wine, happy hour, and Italian food. Fancy a post-dinner drink? Head to Nobody’s Darling for the best cocktails and fun socials, or Hopleaf for locally-brewed artisanal beers.

The staff were welcoming and quick to accommodate any needs I had during my stay, from leaving luggage after check-out to providing a small breakfast treat upon arrival. The classic Windy City weather warnings delayed my arrival by half a day, and the staff was aware of it, and had my room ready for a smooth and warm check in even in the early hours of the morning. Given most of the team are locals, everyone was super knowledgeable about the best places to explore. Stuck for ideas? Ask them.

The hotel has its own fitness room open 24/7 (including Peloton, yoga mats, rowing machine), and wellness treatments which can be delivered directly to your room, such as  HigherDOSE packages including red light face masks ($40) and infra-red sauna blankets ($75) which you can rent for up to 24 hours. If you fancy a refreshing swim, no need to book a pool—Lake Michigan is just under a mile away.

To make the best of two different views of the Windy City, the hotel has two roof decks: one has a skyline view, best enjoyed on clear sky days, and the other faces the tree-tops of the neighborhood. Both are open to guests and free to use. There’s also the club room and library, which can be booked for private events, including bridal or baby showers, and an afternoon tea with a Chicago spin, provided by local Vanille Patisserie. An advance reservation of 72 hours ahead is required, for a minimum party size of 4.

The Guesthouse Hotel straddles Andersonville, the ‘shop local’ district, Ravenswood, known for its breweries, and Uptown, teeming with unassuming yet fantastic restaurants. One such place is Marina’s Bistro & Rum Bar, a blink-and-you-miss-it authentic Puerto Rican spot.

You can spend entire days exploring and shopping in Andersonville, home to over 150 independent businesses from galleries selling local artists’ unique pieces (Andersonville Galleria), record shops (Rattleback Records) and bookshops (Women & Children First), to babywear boutiques (Sandbox Baby Boutique).

If you’re after live shows and musical performances, The Guesthouse is within walking distance from three of the city’s best spots to do so: catch Chicago’s favorite magic show at The Chicago Magic Lounge, or walk to The Riviera Theatre and the Aragon Ballroom, popular venues for big names including AC/DC, Morrissey, and several tribute bands.

When you book a stay at the Guesthouse Hotel, you opt for blending into the neighborhood. The place doesn’t want to be a slick, modern hotel like the ones downtown: its brick-front facade and boutique-like entrance makes this hotel feel like it’s just another house, and if you are after stylish comfort, independence, and that homely feeling, then you won’t find any better.

Just be aware that the hotel requires a two nights minimum stay during peak time (May to end of September) which goes up to three nights during weekends. Low season applies from January to early March, with minimum nights going down to one during the week, and two for weekends.

Price per night: Two beds / two bathrooms suites starting from $550 per night peak season (May-Sep); $275 off-peak (Jan-Mar).

Closest transport: Ravenswood (10 min walk) and Argyle (15 min walk) Metra stops.

You can’t sell what you don’t have. Keeping track of your stock is important and ordering at the right time for the right price helps to keep profits up. To even better use low price opportunities, you can build a warehouse and expand it to allow for larger storage. Keeping a close eye on your stock is crucial as deliveries take time and you really don’t want to run out of goods to sell, not to mention fuel.
